description: Uber, Airbnb, Deliveroo own almost nothing: no cars, no apartments, no employees. How did these platforms become global giants?

hero.hook: Uber has never owned a single car, yet it has disrupted transportation around the world.

blocks.text: Uber, Airbnb, Amazon or Deliveroo belong to a new category of companies: **digital platforms**. They do not just digitize services that already existed: they change the very way of owning, working and being protected.
This model invented a new form of capitalism, which questions our social contract. Let's understand how it works, and why it is so debated.

A traditional company owns factories, vehicles, inventory, and employs employees. A platform breaks this model: it becomes a simple digital infrastructure which connects supply and demand, without producing anything itself.

This system relies on : the more users a platform has, the more useful it becomes, which attracts even more users. For a transportation service, the more drivers available, the shorter the wait, which attracts more customers, who in turn attract more drivers. This circle almost always leads to quasi-monopoly situations. [[Network effect]]
Uber has spent billions of dollars researching self-driving cars, ultimately aiming to get rid of its last big cost: the human driver.

This technical innovation is accompanied by a more contested legal innovation. In the , the platform refuses the status of employer to present itself as a simple technological intermediary, which avoids paying social security contributions, a minimum wage or paid leave. [[Gig economy and uberization]]

blocks.caption: Drivers and delivery people are often classified as self-employed, not employees.

blocks.text: The worker becomes an independent worker who alone bears all the risks: illness, accident, drop in demand. However, it often remains subject to the rules of the application (imposed prices, rating, sanctions), a situation that we call **algorithmic subordination**. Faced with this, courts in several countries have begun to impose the  of these contracts as real salaried employment. [[requalification]]

sections.title: Work without the protections of employment

blocks.text: The impact of these platforms goes beyond the world of work: it is also transforming cities. Airbnb, by facilitating short-term tourist rentals, competes with traditional hotels while reducing the number of accommodations available for residents.

Result: rents are climbing in city centers, and metropolises like Paris or Barcelona have had to impose strict rules, such as quotas for rental days. States are also seeking to establish **digital taxation** so that these platforms pay their share of taxes where they actually earn their money.
In New York, strict regulation against Airbnb in 2023 caused the number of legal listings to drop by 80% in a few months.

The platform economy has brought fast and often less expensive services, and made it easier for some people to find an income. But this effectiveness is based on a weakening of the protections built in the 20th century.

The current debate concerns the creation of an intermediate status, between employee and self-employed, with portability of rights: each worker would accumulate social protections, regardless of the number of platforms for which they work. The future of this model will depend on the ability of regulators to regulate it without stifling innovation.

The platform economy is based on factory-free capitalism that exploits the network effect, while transforming its workers into often precarious freelancers. The battle for better social protections, without breaking this model, has only just begun.

sections.title: Towards a new status for workers?
